items.prompt: What is the halo effect, in the context of interviewing?
choices: A formal scoring bonus given to strong candidates
An early impression coloring the interpretation of everything that follows, even unrelated evidence
A technique interviewers use deliberately to test candidates
A rule requiring interviewers to be positive throughout
items.explanation: The halo effect is an unconscious bias where an early impression shapes how later evidence gets interpreted — not a deliberate technique or formal rule.
items.reference:
Halo effect
early impression forms
colors interpretation of everything after

Why: The interviewer isn't aware it's happening — good intentions don't disable the mechanism.

items.prompt: An interviewer forms a positive impression in the first 90 seconds, then spends the rest of the interview finding the candidate's answers 'confident' and 'clear.' What's the most likely explanation?
choices: The candidate genuinely gave uniformly excellent answers
The halo effect — the early impression is shaping how ambiguous answers get interpreted
The interviewer is being deliberately biased
There's no bias at play, just accurate assessment
items.explanation: This is the halo effect in action — answers of ambiguous quality get read favorably once an early positive impression has formed, without the interviewer intending to be biased.
items.reference:
Halo effect
early impression forms
colors interpretation of everything after

Why: The interviewer isn't aware it's happening — good intentions don't disable the mechanism.

items.prompt: What's the defining difference between an unstructured and a structured interview?
choices: Structured interviews are always shorter
Structured interviews use the same fixed questions and a predefined rubric for every candidate; unstructured interviews improvise both
Unstructured interviews are conducted by more senior interviewers
There's no meaningful difference between the two
items.explanation: The defining feature is fixed questions plus a predefined evaluation standard, applied consistently — not the length, seniority of interviewer, or any other factor.
items.reference:
Unstructured vs. structured
unstructured: improvised, varies per candidate
structured: fixed questions + predefined rubric

Why: A rubric can only fairly compare answers to the same question.

items.prompt: Why does an unstructured interview make it hard to fairly compare two candidates?
choices: Because unstructured interviews are always shorter
Because each candidate effectively takes a different interview, with different questions and no predefined standard for a good answer
Because unstructured interviews require more interviewers
There's no actual difficulty in comparing candidates either way
items.explanation: Without fixed questions and a predefined standard, candidates aren't being measured against the same yardstick, making their scores incomparable even if each individual judgment felt fair.
items.reference:
Unstructured vs. structured
unstructured: improvised, varies per candidate
structured: fixed questions + predefined rubric

Why: A rubric can only fairly compare answers to the same question.

items.prompt: What makes a scoring rubric actually useful, rather than just a numeric label on a gut feeling?
choices: Using a wider numeric scale (e.g. 1-10 instead of 1-5)
Concrete anchors describing what each score level actually requires, decided before any candidate is interviewed
Having the rubric reviewed by HR after the interview
Asking the candidate to self-score their own answer
items.explanation: Concrete, pre-decided anchors are what prevent a numeric score from just being a relabeled gut feeling — without them, a '5' is still whatever the interviewer's intuition says a 5 is.
items.reference:
A rubric anchor
what a 1, 3, or 5 concretely looks like
decided before interviewing anyone

Why: Without concrete anchors, a numeric scale just relabels the same subjective gut feeling.

items.prompt: "Rate the answer 1-5 for problem-solving" is given to interviewers with no further guidance. What's missing?
choices: Nothing — this is already a complete rubric
Concrete anchors describing what a 1, 3, or 5 actually requires in the answer's content
A larger numeric range
Instructions to ask the question faster
items.explanation: Without concrete anchors, this instruction re-introduces the same subjective judgment a rubric is supposed to eliminate — it's a scale with no defined meaning.
items.reference:
A rubric anchor
what a 1, 3, or 5 concretely looks like
decided before interviewing anyone

Why: Without concrete anchors, a numeric scale just relabels the same subjective gut feeling.

items.prompt: If a rubric is well-anchored, does it still matter whether every candidate gets the same questions?
choices: No, a good rubric works regardless of which questions are asked
Yes — a rubric can only fairly compare answers to the same question; different questions make scores incomparable even with identical wording
It only matters for technical roles
It only matters if the interviewer is inexperienced
items.explanation: Even a well-anchored rubric assumes candidates are being compared on the same task — if the underlying questions differ, a matching numeric score doesn't mean the same thing.
items.reference:
Why fixed questions matter
a rubric only compares answers to the SAME question
different questions → scores aren't comparable

Why: Even a perfect rubric can't fairly compare candidates who answered different questions.

items.prompt: An interviewer unconsciously gives an easier version of a question to a candidate they already like. What happens to the fairness of the rubric?
choices: Nothing — the rubric is still fair since the scoring anchors are the same
The comparison breaks down — a 'high score' from an easier question isn't equivalent to the same score from a harder one
This makes the rubric more accurate, not less
This issue only affects unstructured interviews, not structured ones
items.explanation: A rubric's fairness depends on candidates facing the same actual task — subtly varying question difficulty undermines the comparison even with consistent scoring anchors.
items.reference:
Why fixed questions matter
a rubric only compares answers to the SAME question
different questions → scores aren't comparable

Why: Even a perfect rubric can't fairly compare candidates who answered different questions.

items.prompt: Does structured interviewing eliminate an interviewer's personal impressions of a candidate entirely?
choices: Yes, structure makes interviewers feel nothing about candidates
No — it prevents those impressions from silently determining the competency score, but the impression itself can still exist
Yes, but only for very experienced interviewers
No, structure has no effect on personal impressions at all
items.explanation: Structure doesn't switch off human impressions — it stops those impressions from quietly driving the evaluation, anchoring the score to the answer's actual content instead.
items.reference:
What structure doesn't remove
personal impressions can still exist
structure prevents them from silently driving the SCORE

Why: An interviewer can still like a candidate personally — the rubric just stops that feeling from determining the competency evaluation.

items.prompt: An interviewer personally enjoys talking to a candidate more, but structure is in place. Where can that personal impression appropriately go?
choices: It should silently boost the competency score a little
It can be recorded as a separate, explicitly-labeled note (e.g. communication style fit), kept distinct from the technical evaluation
It must be completely suppressed and never recorded anywhere
It should be used to override a low rubric score
items.explanation: The point isn't to pretend the impression doesn't exist — it's to keep it explicitly separate from the competency score rather than letting it silently inflate that score.
items.reference:
What structure doesn't remove
personal impressions can still exist
structure prevents them from silently driving the SCORE

Why: An interviewer can still like a candidate personally — the rubric just stops that feeling from determining the competency evaluation.

items.prompt: What is the general principle behind structured interviewing, beyond hiring specifically?
choices: Always ask the hardest possible questions
Deciding evaluation criteria before seeing the thing being evaluated, rather than after
Interviews should always be conducted by multiple people
Written feedback should always be submitted immediately
items.explanation: The underlying move — fixing criteria in advance — generalizes to any judgment at risk of being shaped by an early impression, not just hiring interviews.
items.reference:
The generalizable move
decide evaluation criteria BEFORE seeing the thing evaluated

Why: This breaks the loop anywhere a first impression could bias which evidence gets sought and how it's interpreted.

items.prompt: A judge at a science fair decides on scoring criteria only after seeing which projects seem most impressive at first glance. What problem does this create?
choices: No problem — this is normal judging practice
The same halo-effect risk as unstructured interviewing: early impressions can shape which criteria get emphasized
This only matters if the judge is inexperienced
Science fairs are immune to this kind of bias
items.explanation: This mirrors the interviewing problem exactly — criteria decided after seeing the candidates (or projects) risks being shaped by the same early-impression bias structured interviewing exists to prevent.
items.reference:
The generalizable move
decide evaluation criteria BEFORE seeing the thing evaluated

Why: This breaks the loop anywhere a first impression could bias which evidence gets sought and how it's interpreted.

items.prompt: A parent decides, before opening either child's report card, exactly what grade range would count as 'needs a conversation' versus 'no concerns.' What principle does this mirror?
choices: This has nothing to do with structured interviewing's principle
Deciding evaluation criteria before seeing the evidence — the same principle behind structured interviewing, applied outside a workplace context
This is actually an example of the halo effect in action
Parents should never set criteria in advance
items.explanation: Fixing the evaluation standard before seeing the actual report card mirrors structured interviewing's core move exactly, just applied to a completely different, non-workplace situation.
items.reference:
The generalizable move
decide evaluation criteria BEFORE seeing the thing evaluated

Why: This breaks the loop anywhere a first impression could bias which evidence gets sought and how it's interpreted.

items.prompt: Why doesn't an interviewer simply trying harder to be objective fix the halo effect?
choices: Because objectivity is impossible in any interview
Because the halo effect operates unconsciously, shaping which questions feel natural and how answers get read, without the interviewer noticing
Because trying harder always makes bias worse
It does fix the problem completely, on its own
items.explanation: The halo effect isn't a conscious choice being made poorly — it's an unconscious shaping of attention and interpretation that good intentions alone don't disable.
items.reference:
Why good intentions don't fix it
halo effect operates unconsciously
trying harder doesn't disable the mechanism

Why: Wanting to be fair just makes the interviewer more confident in a judgment that was never re-examined.

items.prompt: What does 'good intentions make the interviewer more confident in an unexamined judgment' actually mean?
choices: Trying to be fair reduces bias in proportion to effort
Wanting to be objective doesn't force a genuine re-examination of the initial impression — it just adds false confidence to a judgment that was never actually revisited
Good intentions have no relationship to confidence at all
This only applies to inexperienced interviewers
items.explanation: The risk is that sincerely wanting to be fair can create a false sense that bias has been addressed, without the actual mechanism (the early impression shaping later interpretation) ever being interrupted.
items.reference:
Why good intentions don't fix it
halo effect operates unconsciously
trying harder doesn't disable the mechanism

Why: Wanting to be fair just makes the interviewer more confident in a judgment that was never re-examined.

items.prompt: Two interviewers, one who 'tries to be fair' with no structure and one who uses a predefined rubric, evaluate the same candidate. Which is more likely to produce a judgment unaffected by an early impression?
choices: Both are equally likely to be affected, since intent doesn't matter either way
The one using the predefined rubric, since the rubric interrupts the mechanism directly rather than relying on unconscious self-correction
The one who 'tries to be fair,' since intent is what ultimately matters most
Neither — bias is unavoidable regardless of method
items.explanation: A rubric interrupts the actual mechanism (early impression shaping interpretation) structurally, rather than relying on the interviewer's unconscious self-correction, which the unit argues doesn't reliably happen just from good intent.
items.reference:
Why good intentions don't fix it
halo effect operates unconsciously
trying harder doesn't disable the mechanism

Why: Wanting to be fair just makes the interviewer more confident in a judgment that was never re-examined.

items.prompt: Per the L2 flowchart, what determines the final score in the unstructured path?
choices: The rubric anchors
The early impression, which shapes both the follow-up questions and how the answer is interpreted
A vote among multiple interviewers
The candidate's resume alone
items.explanation: In the unstructured path, the early impression flows through to shape questions and interpretation, ultimately producing a score that mirrors that initial impression.
items.reference:
The two paths
unstructured: impression → shaped questions → matching score
structured: fixed questions → rubric → score reflects the answer

Why: Same starting point (a candidate answering a question), two very different mechanisms producing the final score.

items.prompt: Per the L2 flowchart, at what point does the structured path diverge from the unstructured one?
choices: They never diverge — both paths are identical
Immediately — the structured path starts from fixed questions decided in advance rather than an impression-driven improvisation
Only at the very final scoring step
Only if the interviewer is aware of their own bias
items.explanation: The divergence happens at the start — structured interviewing begins from predetermined fixed questions, not from whatever the interviewer's impression makes them want to ask next.
items.reference:
The two paths
unstructured: impression → shaped questions → matching score
structured: fixed questions → rubric → score reflects the answer

Why: Same starting point (a candidate answering a question), two very different mechanisms producing the final score.

items.prompt: In the structured path of the flowchart, what sits between 'fixed questions' and the final score?
choices: Nothing — fixed questions lead directly to a score
The answer being scored against a predefined rubric
A second interviewer's opinion
The candidate's resume
items.explanation: The rubric is the middle step that anchors the score to the answer's actual content — without it, fixed questions alone wouldn't be enough to prevent biased scoring.
items.reference:
The two paths
unstructured: impression → shaped questions → matching score
structured: fixed questions → rubric → score reflects the answer

Why: Same starting point (a candidate answering a question), two very different mechanisms producing the final score.

items.prompt: Per the L2 rubric table, what does a score of 3 require, specifically?
choices: No structured approach at all
A reasonable approach to the problem, but without considering trade-offs or edge cases
A structured approach plus an explicit trade-off plus a validation step
The candidate must mention a specific tool by name
items.explanation: A 3 is the middle anchor — a reasonable approach identified, but missing the trade-off/edge-case consideration that distinguishes a 5.
items.reference:
Applying the rubric table
1: no structured approach
3: reasonable approach, no trade-offs
5: approach + trade-off + validation step

Why: Each level requires something specific and checkable in the answer's content, not a vague overall vibe.

items.prompt: Per the L2 rubric table, what's required to earn a 5 that a 3 doesn't include?
choices: A longer overall answer
At least one explicit trade-off consideration and a concrete way to validate the solution
Mentioning the word 'trade-off' by name
A more confident tone of voice
items.explanation: The 5 anchor specifically requires an explicit trade-off and a validation step — concrete content requirements, not a matter of delivery style or length.
items.reference:
Applying the rubric table
1: no structured approach
3: reasonable approach, no trade-offs
5: approach + trade-off + validation step

Why: Each level requires something specific and checkable in the answer's content, not a vague overall vibe.

items.prompt: A candidate jumps straight to 'I'd just restart the server' with no mention of identifying the actual problem first. Per the L2 rubric table, what score does this earn?
choices: 5, since it's a fast and direct answer
1, since it jumps to a solution without identifying the actual problem
3, since restarting is a reasonable general approach
The rubric has no anchor that covers this case
items.explanation: This matches the 1-anchor exactly: jumping to a solution without first identifying the actual problem — regardless of how confidently or quickly it's delivered.
items.reference:
Applying the rubric table
1: no structured approach
3: reasonable approach, no trade-offs
5: approach + trade-off + validation step

Why: Each level requires something specific and checkable in the answer's content, not a vague overall vibe.

items.prompt: Per the comparison table, why is comparability across candidates low in unstructured interviews?
choices: Because unstructured interviews take less time
Because everyone effectively took a different interview — different questions and no predefined standard for what a good answer looks like
Because unstructured interviews only work for junior roles
There's no actual comparability problem in unstructured interviews
items.explanation: Without a shared question set and a predefined standard, candidates aren't being measured on the same basis — comparability breaks down structurally, not just due to individual bias.
items.reference:
Comparability across candidates
unstructured: low — everyone took a different interview
structured: high — everyone answered the same questions, scored the same way

Why: Fair comparison requires both the same questions AND the same standard for judging answers.

items.prompt: What two things does the comparison table identify as needed for high comparability across candidates?
choices: A longer interview and a panel of interviewers
The same questions and a consistent, predefined standard for scoring answers
A higher salary budget and more candidates
A shorter interview and fewer questions
items.explanation: Both fixed questions and a consistent evaluation standard are required together — either one alone isn't sufficient for genuinely comparable results.
items.reference:
Comparability across candidates
unstructured: low — everyone took a different interview
structured: high — everyone answered the same questions, scored the same way

Why: Fair comparison requires both the same questions AND the same standard for judging answers.

items.prompt: Beyond hiring, which of these is given as an example of the same underlying pattern applying?
choices: Grocery shopping
Code review and performance calibration
Choosing a restaurant
Scheduling a meeting
items.explanation: L2 explicitly names code review and performance calibration as other contexts where deciding evaluation criteria in advance breaks the same early-impression bias loop.
items.reference:
The general shape
criteria decided BEFORE seeing the evidence
not just interviewing — code review, performance calibration, judging

Why: Anywhere a first impression could bias what evidence gets sought and how it's read.

items.prompt: Why does 'deciding criteria before seeing the evidence' work as a general debiasing technique, not just for interviews?
choices: Because it eliminates the need for any human judgment at all
Because it interrupts the same mechanism (an early impression shaping which evidence gets noticed and how it's interpreted) regardless of what's being evaluated
It only works when evaluating people, not projects or code
It works because it makes the evaluation process longer
items.explanation: The mechanism being interrupted — early impressions biasing subsequent evidence-gathering and interpretation — isn't specific to interviewing, so the fix generalizes to any similar evaluation context.
items.reference:
The general shape
criteria decided BEFORE seeing the evidence
not just interviewing — code review, performance calibration, judging

Why: Anywhere a first impression could bias what evidence gets sought and how it's read.

items.prompt: In the worked example's unstructured version, why does the interviewer rate Candidate A's generic answer favorably?
choices: Because the answer was genuinely more detailed than Candidate B's
Because the interviewer already liked Candidate A from the first minute, and reads the fluent-but-generic answer as confident and competent
Because Candidate A used more technical vocabulary
Because Candidate A answered the question faster
items.explanation: The favorable reading comes from the pre-existing impression, not from the answer's actual content — the answer itself was described as fluent but generic.
items.reference:
The unstructured outcome
Candidate A: generic answer, read favorably (liked already)
Candidate B: specific answer, read as uncertain (hesitant delivery)

Why: The interviewer's early impression, not the answer content, determined the direction of the judgment.

items.prompt: What specifically does the interviewer misread about Candidate B's answer in the unstructured version?
choices: The interviewer correctly identifies it as the stronger answer
The interviewer perceives the hesitant delivery as uncertainty and doesn't register that the content (specific correlation strategy, deploy bisection) was more rigorous
Candidate B's answer was actually less detailed than Candidate A's
The interviewer doesn't listen to Candidate B's answer at all
items.explanation: The misread is specifically about conflating delivery confidence with answer quality — the content was more specific and rigorous, but the hesitant delivery obscured that from the biased interviewer.
items.reference:
The unstructured outcome
Candidate A: generic answer, read favorably (liked already)
Candidate B: specific answer, read as uncertain (hesitant delivery)

Why: The interviewer's early impression, not the answer content, determined the direction of the judgment.

items.prompt: What do the written feedback comments ('strong communicator, clearly experienced' vs. 'answer was a bit unclear') actually reflect, per the worked example?
choices: An accurate summary of each answer's technical content
The interviewer's early impression and reaction to delivery style, not a genuine assessment of the answers' substance
Formal scores from a rubric applied after the interview
Feedback written by a second, independent interviewer
items.explanation: The feedback mirrors the pre-existing impression almost exactly — it reflects delivery-driven reactions, not the substantive comparison the structured version later reveals.
items.reference:
The unstructured outcome
Candidate A: generic answer, read favorably (liked already)
Candidate B: specific answer, read as uncertain (hesitant delivery)

Why: The interviewer's early impression, not the answer content, determined the direction of the judgment.

items.prompt: In the worked example's structured version, why does Candidate A score a 3 rather than a 5?
choices: Because Candidate A's delivery was too confident
Because the answer (check logs, look at deploys, narrow it down) is a reasonable approach but names no specific correlation strategy, trade-off, or validation step
Because the interviewer personally dislikes Candidate A
Because Candidate A ran out of time
items.explanation: The score is determined purely by matching the answer's content against the rubric's anchors — Candidate A's answer meets the 3-level bar but not the 5-level requirements.
items.reference:
The structured outcome
Candidate A: reasonable approach, no trade-off/validation → 3
Candidate B: approach + explicit trade-off + validation → 5

Why: Scored against the same predefined anchors, the outcome reverses.

items.prompt: What specific element of Candidate B's answer earns the explicit 'trade-off' requirement for a score of 5?
choices: Mentioning logs at all
Explicitly preferring targeted logging over repeated redeploys — a stated trade-off against a less precise alternative
Speaking more confidently than Candidate A
Using more technical jargon
items.explanation: The trade-off requirement is met by Candidate B explicitly weighing targeted logging against redeploying repeatedly — a concrete, checkable trade-off, not a vague impression.
items.reference:
The structured outcome
Candidate A: reasonable approach, no trade-off/validation → 3
Candidate B: approach + explicit trade-off + validation → 5

Why: Scored against the same predefined anchors, the outcome reverses.

items.prompt: Under the structured scoring, does Candidate B's more hesitant delivery style factor into the final rubric score at all?
choices: Yes, hesitant delivery automatically lowers the score by one point
No — the rubric anchors are defined entirely in terms of answer content (approach, trade-off, validation), not delivery style
Yes, but only for the trade-off criterion specifically
The rubric doesn't specify either way
items.explanation: The rubric's anchors are content-based, which is exactly why Candidate B's hesitant delivery — irrelevant to the anchors — doesn't affect the score, unlike in the unstructured version.
items.reference:
The structured outcome
Candidate A: reasonable approach, no trade-off/validation → 3
Candidate B: approach + explicit trade-off + validation → 5

Why: Scored against the same predefined anchors, the outcome reverses.

What structure doesn't erase
personal preference can still exist

items.prompt: Per the extension question, what happens if a well-structured interview process uses a badly-designed rubric?
choices: Structure automatically corrects any rubric design flaws

This scenario is impossible — good structure always implies a good rubric
The interview simply becomes invalid and produces no score at all
items.explanation: Structure guarantees consistency and comparability, not correctness — a flawed rubric applied consistently still yields a systematically biased result, just a different kind of bias.

The extension question

Why: Structure changes WHERE the bias lives (in the rubric, not the gut) — it doesn't guarantee the bias is gone.

items.prompt: What does the extension question recommend as a safeguard against a badly-designed rubric, rather than abandoning structure altogether?

Treating rubric design as its own thing worth getting right, ideally reviewed by more than one person before use on real candidates
Using a much longer rubric with more score levels
Letting each interviewer write their own personal rubric
items.explanation: The fix isn't discarding structure — it's applying real scrutiny (ideally multiple reviewers) to the rubric's design itself, before it's used to evaluate real candidates.
items.reference:
The extension question
structure ≠ automatically correct
a badly-designed rubric still produces biased outcomes

Why: Structure changes WHERE the bias lives (in the rubric, not the gut) — it doesn't guarantee the bias is gone.

items.prompt: A rubric happens to reward a specific debugging technique that only candidates who've seen a very similar past incident would know. What kind of problem does this illustrate?

A rubric design flaw — consistent application doesn't fix a rubric that unfairly favors a narrow, coincidental prior experience over general skill
This proves structured interviewing doesn't work and should be abandoned
This is only a problem if the rubric is publicly shared with candidates in advance

items.reference:
The extension question
structure ≠ automatically correct
a badly-designed rubric still produces biased outcomes

Why: Structure changes WHERE the bias lives (in the rubric, not the gut) — it doesn't guarantee the bias is gone.

Recognizing the failure modes

deciding anchors after seeing the answer

Why: Each failure mode breaks a specific link between the rubric and a fair, comparable score.
